name: IRIAF F-4E Phantom II
service: Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force (IRIAF)

serviceWindow.statusNotes: Iran received its first F-4Es in 1971 and ordered 177 in total. The fleet is old and short of spares. Open sources put about 60 F-4D, F-4E and RF-4E aircraft in service as of 2021, but how many can fly today is not publicly known. Reports describe a crash on 19 February 2026 and a strike at Tabriz on 1 March 2026. Treat the numbers, equipment fit and readiness as uncertain.

propulsionSummary: Two General Electric J79-GE-17A afterburning turbojets, each rated at 17,845 lbf (about 79 kN) with afterburner.

weapons.name: AIM-7E Sparrow
weapons.mountSummary: Four missiles in semi-recessed bays under the fuselage. Iranian stocks and the exact Sparrow variant in use are not confirmed.

weapons.name: AIM-9P Sidewinder
weapons.mountSummary: Carried on inboard wing pylons. Iranian stocks and the exact Sidewinder variant in use are not confirmed.

sensors.name: AN/APQ-120 radar
sensors.role: Air search and fire control for Sparrow missiles, with air-to-ground ranging

sensors.name: AN/APR-36 radar warning receiver (original US fit)
sensors.role: Passive detection of hostile radar emissions. The Iranian aircraft's current fit is unconfirmed.

sensors.name: Crew visual lookout
sensors.role: Visual identification of aircraft and ships in clear weather

loadouts.name: Air defence fit
loadouts.role: Intercept and combat air patrol with radar and infrared missiles

loadouts.name: Anti-armour or anti-ship strike with Maverick
loadouts.role: Close air support or attack on small boats using TV-guided missiles

radar.note: A large twin-engine 1950s-design airframe with an unshaped intake and many external stores, which gives a strong radar return.

infrared.note: Two J79 afterburning turbojets are strong heat sources, especially from behind.

visual.note: A large airframe. The later smokeless J79-17C and -17E engines removed the dark smoke trail, but the Iranian engine fit is unconfirmed.

brief.whatItIs: The F-4E Phantom II is a big twin-engine American jet from the 1960s that served as both a fighter and a bomber. It carries a pilot and a weapons officer, an internal 20 mm cannon, and a heavy load of missiles and bombs. Iran bought a large fleet in the 1970s and still flies a shrinking number of them today.
brief.howItIsUsed: A commander in this scenario would use Iranian Phantoms as a low-end strike and patrol force, not as a front-line air defence fighter. Their radar is old and range is limited, so they work best near friendly ground radars and against targets that cannot shoot back well. They can fly low over water to attack ships and boats with Maverick missiles or unguided weapons. Against a modern US Navy fighter with an AESA radar and AMRAAM missiles, a Phantom is outranged and easy to detect. Spare parts are scarce, so sortie rates are low and a commander should expect many aircraft to be unavailable on any given day.
typicalMissions: Low-level strike on ships and small craft
Close air support for ground forces
Combat air patrol near friendly territory
